NBC sportscaster Dan Hicks, who covered golf, Olympic swimming and Notre Dame football over the course of his decades-long career, died on Nov. 11 of a lung infection.

On Tuesday, the California Post confirmed it had obtained a copy of Hicks’ death certificate, which listed the 64-year-old’s cause of death as multifocal pneumonia. His passing was deemed natural.

The document also noted that Hicks had also been dealing with a pulmonary edema, or fluid buildup in his lungs, that was preceded by an upper respiratory infection as well as autoimmune hemolytic anemia.

While standard pneumonia usually affects one area of the lungs, multifocal pneumonia can involve multiple regions of the lungs becoming inflamed and infected at the same time, making it more challenging to diagnose and treat. It is considered more severe and serious than its localized counterpart.

Hicks was pronounced dead on the evening of Nov. 11 at a hospital near his home in Greenwich, Connecticut.

Hicks’ wife, Hannah Storm, released a statement that day noting she and his family members were “heartbroken by [Hicks’] sudden and unexpected passing.”

“He was a devoted husband of over 30 years, loving father to our three daughters, and cherished friend to so many,” her statement continued, according to The Associated Press. “His loss is immeasurable.”

“In his 34 years at NBC Sports, he was an exceptional storyteller and caller of games and events who elevated some of the biggest moments in sports history,” their statement read. “But far beyond his on-air excellence, Dan was a better person who welcomed teammates with a smile, a joke, or a word of encouragement, sometimes all three in the same sentence.”

Speaking to the AP at the start of his 35th season at NBC Sports in September, Hicks said he felt “incredibly lucky” to still be working in sports journalism, despite the many changes in media he’d witnessed over the course of his career.

“It takes a lot of things going your way as far as NBC continuing to have the properties that I’ve been a part of through the years,” he explained. “So lots of variables, lots of things that can happen in your career. But I think I appreciate it more and more the longer it’s been.”

In his addition to his wife, Hicks is survived by daughters Hannah, Ellery and Riley.
